title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Stateless Specification
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol project shipped its most significant specification revision since MCP launched in November 2024. The **2026-07-28 spec** breaks with MCP's original stateful, sticky-session design — the core protocol changes are backward-incompatible, reflecting lessons the maintainers say they learned over the two years since launch. This page covers what changed and why; see the Tool Use & Agents page for MCP's original architecture (server/client/transport model), which still holds at a high level.

---

## The Core Change: Stateless Protocol

Previously, a remote MCP server typically needed:

- **Sticky sessions** — a client's requests had to keep hitting the same server instance
- **A shared session store** — to keep session state consistent if requests did land on different instances
- **Deep packet inspection at the gateway** — to route protocol-aware traffic correctly

Under the new stateless core, a remote MCP server can instead run behind a **plain round-robin load balancer**, because there's no server-side session affinity to preserve. Two accompanying features make this practical:

- **Header-based routing** — an `Mcp-Method` header lets infrastructure route a request by method without deep-inspecting the JSON-RPC body
- **Cacheable list results** — responses to calls like `tools/list` can now be cached, since they no longer depend on hidden per-session state

---

## Other Additions

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span more than one request/response pair, useful for flows that need an intermediate step (e.g., elicitation) without holding a session open
- **Authorization hardening** — stronger OAuth and OIDC support, building on the authorization model MCP introduced in earlier revisions
- **A formal extensions framework** — versioned extensions (the spec calls out **Apps** and **Tasks** as examples) let optional functionality evolve independently of the core spec instead of being crammed into it
- **Updated Tier 1 SDKs** — the reference SDKs were updated to implement the new core before the spec's general release

---

## Governance Changes

Alongside the technical revision, MCP's governance matured:

- A formal **Contributor Ladder** defines how contributors gain standing in the project
- **Working Groups** now triage Spec Enhancement Proposals (SEPs) within their own area, rather than routing everything through one central review
- The specification now has an explicit **feature lifecycle and deprecation policy**, so breaking changes like this one follow a documented process going forward
- On August 22, 2026, the Core Maintainers published an updated roadmap for the *next* specification release, developed jointly with the Working Groups

---

## Why It Matters for Builders

The practical upshot for anyone running an MCP server in production: infrastructure gets simpler. A server that previously needed session-aware load balancing and a shared state store can be deployed behind commodity round-robin infrastructure. For client authors (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and others), the header-based routing and cacheable list results reduce redundant round-trips when discovering what tools a server exposes.

Adoption is broad: by mid-2026, MCP is used not just by Anthropic's own products but by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and thousands of development teams, with AWS named as a committed infrastructure partner for the ecosystem. The number of public MCP servers has grown well past the "hundreds" figure cited when MCP was new (see Tool Use & Agents), spanning databases (Postgres, Redis), productivity suites, and enterprise systems.

---

## Related: Claude's MCP Support

Claude's own MCP client support tracks the new spec closely — as of August 2026 it supports the 2026-07-28 spec's stateless core plus connector-level features like embedded UI, enterprise-managed auth, observability, and private network tunnels. Claude's Microsoft 365 connector, for example, gained write tools in the same period (drafting/sending email, managing calendar events, editing OneDrive/SharePoint files), built on this updated connector infrastructure.
